description:
AMD's Radeon RX 6700 XT video card releases March 18. This is our review & benchmark of the new RX 6700 XT GPU, particularly vs. the RTX 3060 & RTX 3070 cards.
Sponsor: Buy Thermaltake's Tower 100 Mini-ITX case on Amazon (https://geni.us/TuAASGt)

Watch our review of the RTX 3060: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3C-RoDtqdJ8
Watch our warning signs about buying used GPUs here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J2VkkEHDG5E&
Watch our Intel i7-11700K benchmarks here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AgFlB0HG_84

Our GN Tear-Down Toolkits and Wireframe Desk Mouse Mats are in stock & shipping: https://store.gamersnexus.net/

Our review of the AMD RX 6700 XT tests the card versus the other recent releases on the market (and some old - like the GTX 1080 Ti, RTX 2070, RTX 2080 Super, RTX 2060, et al), establishing which GPU is the "best" for 2021 thus far. Unfortunately, the answer seems largely the same as previous times we've answered this lately: Whichever you can get. There's one major problem with the 6700 XT, though, and it's the same that the RTX 3060 had: It's greedily positioned, and so once again we end up with a product which fails to move the needle meaningfully over previous generations, like the RX 5700 XT.

RELATED PRODUCTS

The mythical AMD RX 6700 XT will be on Amazon one day: https://geni.us/pcwx

comments.text:
TBH, the benchmarks do not correlate with the title of the video. This card as advertised for 1440p, is actually good enough in that res and equivalent to the RTX 3070 based on the numbers here. Some games like SOTTR, Ubisoft Open Worlds, etc. are better with AMD while some others like RDR2 and Cyberpunk are with NVIDIA, but that averages out. Other aspects like power consumption etc. are also comparable. They targeted the 3070, and it shows. 

Now, even if the 3070 is better in 4k, remember that it does not achieve 60 FPS, so it is unplayable and that delta improvement does not matter. Theoretical numbers do not translate to real world usage. If I get 55 fps with 3070 and 50 with 6700 XT, neither are playable at 4k (nor were they designed to be). 4k gamers are anyway going to start at 8 series onwards from either camp.

Coming to the MSRP set by the manufacturers, note that this has increased generation-wise on NVIDIA side also, so we cannot single out the Reds here. The 7 series on Green camp was $330 (GTX 970), $400 (GTX 1070), and now $500 for the 3070. So not too far off from AMD's $80 increase from 5700 XT.

comments.text:
I think what matters most is just that, i.e. what's in stock, and how is it vs other cards also in stock, and which is a better value in terms of performance/scalped price ratio at current prices that wont go down anytime in 2021. These days we have to take what we can get. Benchmarks help us decide between two cards for the same price, and between a cheaper card vs one that costs more, and the price now is what matters. I'm not happy paying 2x or 3x more for an RTX with 25% to 50% better performance if the cheaper card is actually playable at over 50-60 fps on a freesync/g-sync monitor.

What I saw in the video was that in non-RTX gaming that the 6700 XT was often keeping up with the 3070, but my $799 6700 XT was half the cost of a scalped RTX 3070 that cost $1500-1800 right now. Also, my 6700 XT is as fast (and often faster) than my son's previous MSI 2080 Super from May 2020 at the same price (2080S was before he got a 3080 for $800 in a VRLA built PC that he bought in November and delivered in January). 

Sure, the 6700 XT should have been $470-480, and therefore in a perfect world I'd buy a RTX 3070 at $500 before I ever bought a 6700 XT (if I had that choice). Actually, I'd buy a RTX 3080 for $800 in a perfect world, and not pay $2000+ for a scalped 3080or $800 for a scalped 6700 XT. We laughed at buyers and sellers last October who were dealing with $1600 for a 3080 at 2x MSRP - we had no idea that 6 months later they would cost 3x MSRP. We were waiting for prices to come down, and could have lost 6 months of getting to game on a nicer card.

comments.text: How much are the new Tariffs impacting the MSRP of this card? Those tariffs did not exist when the 6800/6800XT/3060 Ti/3070/3080, right? Weren't the Trump Tariff's 25% on Motherboards and GPU's? While I'm not at all impressed by the generational improvement here either, but comparing the 6700 XT to the 5700 XT MSRP doesn't seem to be fair, when the 6700 XT's MSRP of $479 seemingly factors in at least $80 worth of tariff that did not exist with the 5700 XT. So, the 5700 XT was $399 MSRP at launch, if you apply the 25% tariff to that, you get $499, so unless I'm missing something, doesn't it appear that the price of the 6700 XT before the 25% tariff is actually closer to $384, which is LESS than the MSRP of the pre-tariff 5700 XT? I'm taking no sides here, but I'm curious how much impact the tariffs have on pricing, and when you compare the performance uplift value w/out tariff's, is the generational improvement really as bad as it looks here? Steve, a few issues. SAM/Rebar is not giving the same performance boost on AMD vs Nvidia cards. (Hypothetically, in the future, Nvidia can get it working similarly, but hypothetically AMD will have a DLSS competitor...)

Second, it’s worth commenting on driver overhead bottlenecking of weaker CPU performance, as recently highlighted again by Hardware Unboxed. Many of us have older CPUs as it’s difficult to upgrade right now, and are running into cpu bottlenecks where a 6700xt will outperform a 3080 because of the cpu bottle neck, or other crazy situations. comments.text:
I believe you're talking about the error bars.  I don't know how seriously GN takes them, or how they're calculated here, so I don't really know if they're worth anything.  In the worst case, at least they're designed to show that the results aren't perfectly precise but performance can reasonably be expected to be within those limits.  So if you have 2 cards and one has a higher score, but the error bars are overlapping, you can't really even say for sure that it's a slightly better card.  

An easy to understand example would be measuring things with a ruler.  Maybe you can measure something to be, say, 25cm ± ["plus or minus"] 0.5mm.  So you would have a chart with 250mm and an 'H' from 249.5-250.5.  Interestingly, or, if you have to deal with these things seriously in practice, very very boringly, if you measure 2 things, say 12cm and 13cm and you add them to get the 25cm result, then the same ±0.5mm for each measurement will become √(0.5^2 + 0.5^2) which is about ±0.7mm.  Things can get a bit more complicated than this if you're not just adding 2 simple errors.

The idea is that you make a chip with a smaller die, so that you can make a lot more of them.
The problem is that RT cores and infinity cache waste a lot of space, so the new die in the 6700xt isn't that much smaller than a 6900xt. RTX chips are also way bigger and more power hungry compared to previous generations thanks to all the RT and Tensor bloat. 

I would love if one of the companies came out with a smaller/simpler low-end GPU that could be made cheaply in massive quantities, but neither of them have much reason to do that right now. The margins are higher on the big GPUs. You have to build/ship and sell ten $150 GPUs to make up for one $1500 gpu
